title: To the River
text:
Beautiful river! In your clear and shining wave

of crystal, wandering water, you are an emblem

of beauty's splendor, an emblem of the heart

that does not hide itself now, an emblem

of art's joyful fantasy in the house of old

Albert's daughter.


--


But while she gazes into your current,-which

shines and trembles, why does the most

beautiful of all rivers remind one of its

worshipers? It is because in her heart, as in

your wave, her image is deeply engraved;

in her heart that trembles beneath the brightness of

her soul-searching eyes!
editorial_note: The translation follows the Spanish Poe text's emblematic river and its reflection of the beloved.

title: To Miss ***
text:
The shaded bowers beneath which I see, in my dreams,

the most playful songbirds, are

lips; and all the melody of your voice is made

only by words created by your lips.


--


From your eyes, set in the heavenly sanctuary

of your heart, desolate glances fall

now, oh God!, upon my funereal spirit,

like the light of a star upon a shroud.


--


Your heart, your heart! I wake and

sigh, and go back to sleep so I may dream

until the day of truth, which gold,-capable of

so many follies,-will never be able to buy.
editorial_note: The translation keeps this fuller Spanish variant of Poe's bower-and-eyes address.

title: Because I Feel That in the Heavens...
text:
Because I feel that in the heavens

the angels, whispering among themselves,

find among their burning words of love

none so devout as that of "mother."


Long have I called you by that dear name,

you who are more than a mother to me,

because you fill the heart of my heart, where death placed you

when it set free the spirit of my beloved Virginia.


My mother, my own mother, dead early,

was only my mother; but you are the mother

of the woman I loved so much,


and so you are dearer than the mother I knew,

by that eternity with which my soul

idolized my wife more than its own soul.
editorial_note: The translation repairs the source's broken quote around 'mother' while preserving the Spanish text's elegiac address.

title: Sonnet to Science
text:
Science! True daughter of time you are,

you who alter all things

with your searching eyes.

Why do you devour the poet's heart so,

vulture, whose wings are dull realities?


How should he love you? Or how can he judge you wise,

he whom you do not let wander

in search of treasure in the jeweled heavens,

though he rose on intrepid wing?


Have you not snatched Diana from her chariot?

Nor driven the Hamadryads from the wood

to seek shelter in some happy star?


Have you not torn the Naiads from the flood,

the Elf from the green grass, and me

from the summer dream beneath the tamarind?
editorial_note: The catalog title is generic, but the visible body is 'Sonnet to Science'; the translation follows that body.
